name: Microservices
tagline: An API gateway, independently deployable services with their own data, and async events
summary: Clients reach every service through one API gateway that authenticates, rate-limits and routes. Each service owns its database and never reads another service's tables; state changes are shared as events over RabbitMQ so services stay decoupled and can be deployed independently.

nodes.label: Web / Mobile Client
nodes.why: Talks to one public hostname; it does not know how many services exist behind it.

nodes.label: API Gateway
nodes.why: Cross-cutting concerns live in one place: verify the JWT, enforce per-client limits, route /orders and /inventory to the right service.

nodes.label: Auth Service
nodes.why: Issues and validates tokens so other services never handle passwords.

nodes.label: Order Service
nodes.why: Owns the order lifecycle and its database; publishes OrderCreated instead of calling inventory directly.

nodes.label: Inventory Service
nodes.why: Reserves stock in response to order events and exposes stock queries; can be scaled and deployed without touching orders.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: The gateway and auth service need sub-millisecond lookups for revoked tokens and request counters.

nodes.label: RabbitMQ
nodes.why: Routes OrderCreated, StockReserved and PaymentFailed to the services that subscribe, with acknowledgements and dead-letter queues built in.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL (auth)
nodes.why: Private to the auth service; no other service can read password hashes.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL (orders)
nodes.why: Relational integrity for orders and lines; the outbox table lets events be published only for committed orders.

nodes.label: MongoDB (inventory)
nodes.why: Stock per SKU per warehouse is a flat, high-write document; the team chose a document store and can change it without affecting anyone else.

nodes.label: Notification Worker
nodes.why: Subscribes to order events and calls providers; retries and dead-letters failures without involving the order service.

flows.name: Place an order
steps: The client POSTs /orders with its JWT.
The gateway verifies the token, checks the rate limit and routes to the order service.
The order service validates the request and creates the order as PENDING.
Order and OrderCreated outbox row are committed in one transaction; the client gets 202 Accepted.
RabbitMQ delivers OrderCreated to every subscribed queue.
The inventory service consumes it idempotently and reserves stock.
The reservation is written to MongoDB and StockReserved is published back for the order service to confirm the order.

flows.name: Log in and cache the token
steps: The gateway forwards to the auth service without needing a token.
The auth service verifies the password hash.
Token metadata is cached in Redis so later requests are verified at the gateway without hitting the auth database.

flows.name: Notify without coupling
steps: The order service publishes OrderConfirmed — it has no idea who listens.
RabbitMQ routes a copy to the notifications queue.
The worker sends the email; on provider failure it retries with backoff and finally dead-letters the message.

decisions.decision: One API gateway in front of all services
decisions.why: Authentication, rate limiting, TLS and routing are implemented once instead of in every service, and clients see a single stable API.
decisions.tradeoff: The gateway is a single point of failure and a shared deploy; a plain load balancer per service is simpler but pushes auth and limits into every codebase.

decisions.why: A service can change its schema, scale its store or switch database technology without coordinating with other teams. Inventory chose MongoDB; orders stayed on PostgreSQL.
decisions.tradeoff: No cross-service joins or transactions: reports need data copied via events, and multi-service operations need a saga. A single shared PostgreSQL is far simpler while the team is small.

decisions.decision: Asynchronous events over synchronous REST chains
decisions.why: If the order service called inventory, then payment, then notifications in sequence, every downstream outage would fail order placement. Events let each consumer fail and recover on its own.
decisions.tradeoff: Eventual consistency and harder debugging: an order is PENDING until inventory reacts, and a request no longer has a single call stack to trace.

decisions.why: Traffic is moderate, routing keys map cleanly onto per-service queues, and built-in acknowledgements and dead-letter exchanges cover the failure handling needed.
decisions.tradeoff: No long-term replay: a new service cannot rebuild its state from history. If event volume grows or replay becomes important, Kafka is the natural move.

versions.title: Monolith
versions.summary: One application with one database handles users, orders and stock.

versions.title: Gateway and auth extracted
versions.summary: Authentication becomes its own service with a private database; a gateway verifies tokens and rate-limits using Redis.

versions.title: Inventory extracted
versions.summary: Inventory gets its own service and a document store chosen for its access pattern.

versions.title: Async events
versions.summary: Services stop calling each other synchronously; RabbitMQ carries events and a notification worker consumes them.

textAlternative: A client at the top sends HTTPS requests with a JWT to an API gateway. The gateway routes to three services in a row below it: an auth service on the left, an order service in the middle and an inventory service on the right. Each service has its own database at the bottom: PostgreSQL for auth, PostgreSQL for orders and MongoDB for inventory. Redis, below the auth service, caches tokens and rate-limit counters. RabbitMQ on the right receives events from the order and inventory services and delivers them to the inventory service and a notification worker.
